title: The More Things Change
goals: Close the course by integrating the advanced C1 and C2 structures: inversion, cleft sentences, mixed and inverted conditionals, subjunctive and concessives.
Talk about social and technological change with precise vocabulary: tipping point, entrenched, obsolete, digital divide.
Use proverbs and cultural allusions naturally and without cliché (Pandora's box, Achilles' heel, old habits die hard).
Structure an oral presentation: open, move from one point to another, concede, qualify and close.
Reflect in writing on change and continuity with a mature, well-cohesive register.
Synthesise readings and debates: reconstruct arguments and take a position with nuance.

learn.title: Subject–auxiliary inversion (full review)
learn.html:
When an adverb or phrase of negative, restrictive or emphatic meaning opens the sentence, the subject and auxiliary invert, as in a question. If there is no auxiliary, one is added do / does / did. The effect is solemn or literary emphasis; in a speech or essay it adds rhythm and authority.

AperturaEstructuraEjemplo
Never, rarely, seldom, scarcely ever, little+ aux + subject + past participle / verbRarely have we seen such a rapid transformation. Little did they know that the factory would close.
Not only … (but also)Not only + aux + subject …Not only did the reform fail; it also deepened inequality.
Hardly / Scarcely … when / before; No sooner … thanHad + subject + past participle, + when / thanNo sooner had the law passed than critics began to object.
Under no circumstances, On no account, In no way, At no point+ aux + subjectUnder no circumstances should the data be shared.
Only when / after / by / then; Not until+ aux + subject (in the main clause)Only after the crisis did the government act. Not until the data leaked did the firm apologise.
So + adj / Such + noun … thatSo rapid was the change that …Such was the pace of change that nobody could keep up.
Nor / Neither / Nor did+ aux + subjectThe plan was costly; nor was it popular.
  • The inversion affects the main clause: Not until the system collapsed did anyone question it; the subordinate clause (the system collapsed) keeps the normal order.
  • If the negative adverb does not open the sentence, there is no inversion: We have rarely seen…
  • Inversion with only and not until is the one Spanish speakers get wrong most often, because Spanish does not invert.

watch.wrong: Never I have seen such a dramatic shift.
watch.right: Never have I seen such a dramatic shift.
watch.why: After Never at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject.

watch.wrong: Not until the data leaked, the company apologised.
watch.right: Not until the data leaked did the company apologise.
watch.why: The main verb takes did; the verb returns to its base form.

watch.wrong: Hardly he had arrived when the meeting began.
watch.right: Hardly had he arrived when the meeting began.
watch.why: Hardly + had + subject + past participle; completed with when.

watch.wrong: Only then I understood the problem.
watch.right: Only then did I understand the problem.
watch.why: Only + a time adverb at the start requires inversion with do/did.

learn.title: Cleft sentences and emphasis
learn.html:
Cleft sentences (cleft sentences) split a statement into two parts to focus on one element. They are English's tool for what Spanish achieves with word order or intonation.

TipoEstructuraEjemplo
It-cleftIt is/was + foco + that / who …It was the printing press that transformed European society. It is not until you try it that you understand.
Wh-cleft (pseudo-hendida)What + clause + is/was + focusWhat worries me most is the speed of the change.
Inverted wh-cleftFoco + is/was + what …The speed of the change is what worries me most.
All / The thing / The reason whyAll (that) I … is …; The reason why … is that …All I ask is that you give it a fair hearing. The reason why it failed is that nobody explained it.
Emphasis with do / didsubject + do/does/did + base verbI do appreciate the effort, even if the results disappoint.
  • Who for people, that for things, places and times: It was in 2007 that the first smartphone appeared (not when).
  • In wh-clefts, the part with what works as the subject: What I need is more time, with no repeated pronoun (What I need it is is a mistake).
  • With what, the verb be agrees with the focus: What we need are clear rules (also acceptable: is).

watch.wrong: It was in 2007 when the first smartphone appeared.
watch.right: It was in 2007 that the first smartphone appeared.
watch.why: In the it-cleft the second part is introduced by that, not by when.

watch.wrong: What I need it is more time.
watch.right: What I need is more time.
watch.why: What already acts as the object; the pronoun is not repeated.

watch.wrong: It is the council who decide the budget.
watch.right: It is the council that decides the budget.
watch.why: If the focus is an institution (a thing), it takes that and a singular verb.

watch.wrong: The reason because it failed is that nobody explained it.
watch.right: The reason why it failed is that nobody explained it.
watch.why: The reason why …, not because.

learn.title: Mixed conditionals, inverted conditionals and wish / if only
learn.html:
Beyond the three basic types, a competent speaker mixes tenses to link past and present, and inverts to sound formal.

TipoEstructuraEjemplo
Mixed: past cause → present effectIf + past perfect, would + base verbIf I had accepted that job, I would be living in Berlin now.
Mixed: permanent present condition → past effectIf + past simple, would have + past participleIf she weren't so stubborn, she would have been promoted.
Inversion (past)Had + subject + past participle …Had I known the risks, I would have acted differently.
Inversion (improbable hypothesis)Were + subject + to + verb; Should + subject + verbWere the plan to fail, we'd start again. Should you need help, ask.
wish / if only + pastwish about the presentI wish I knew the answer. If only we had more time.
wish / if only + past perfectregret about the pastI wish I had listened. If only they hadn't left.
wish + wouldcomplaint about someone else's behaviourI wish you would stop interrupting.
It's (high) time / would rather + pastpresent with an unreal meaningIt's high time the government did something. I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.
  • Never would in the if-clause (except for politeness: If you would wait here…). Tampoco wish … would have: I wish he had listened, not would have listened.
  • Wish … would is not used with one's own subject: you do not say I wish I would.
  • With were in all persons (If I were you) the register is formal; If I was is common in spoken language.

watch.wrong: If I would have known, I would have told you.
watch.right: If I had known, I would have told you.
watch.why: The if-clause takes the past perfect, never would have.

watch.wrong: I wish he would have listened to our warnings.
watch.right: I wish he had listened to our warnings.
watch.why: Regret about the past: wish + past perfect.

watch.wrong: It's high time the government does something.
watch.right: It's high time the government did something.
watch.why: It's time + past simple (unreal meaning).

watch.wrong: I'd rather you don't tell anyone.
watch.right: I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.
watch.why: Would rather + different subject + past simple.

learn.title: The subjunctive in English
learn.html:
The English subjunctive is almost invisible because it matches the base form of the verb, but it is still alive in formal, legal and journalistic register. There are three main uses.

UseFormExample
Mandative: after demand, insist, propose, recommend, suggest, require; after essential, vital, imperative, crucial, important, desirablethat + subject + base verb (no -s, no will). Negative: that + subject + not + base. British English allows should.It is essential that every candidate be informed. The committee demanded that the report be published. I insisted that she not travel alone.
Unreal with were: if, as if / as though, wish, supposewere for all personsIf I were you, I'd think twice. He talks as if he were the owner.
Fixed formulasinherited base formLong live the king. God forbid. Suffice it to say … Be that as it may. Come what may. So be it. Far be it from me to criticise.
  • Spanish requires the subjunctive after “es importante que…”; everyday English replaces it with should (It's important that he should know) or with an infinitive structure (It's important for him to know).
  • The mandative subjunctive sounds natural in American English; in formal British English should. Both are correct, but the form indicative (that he is informed) is incorrect in careful register.
  • After suggest, recommend and propose is not used with person + to: She recommended that he apply, not She recommended him to apply.

watch.wrong: It is vital that he is informed of the decision.
watch.right: It is vital that he be informed of the decision.
watch.why: Mandative subjunctive: base verb, also with be.

watch.wrong: The committee demanded that the report was published.
watch.right: The committee demanded that the report be published.
watch.why: After demand: subjunctive (be published) or should be published.

watch.wrong: I insisted that she doesn't travel alone.
watch.right: I insisted that she not travel alone.
watch.why: Negation of the subjunctive: not + base verb, without do.

watch.wrong: She recommended him to apply.
watch.right: She recommended that he apply.
watch.why: Recommend is not built with person + to.

learn.title: Concesivas: Much as, Try as they might, Albeit, Be that as it may
learn.html:
Concessive structures acknowledge a fact that seems to contradict the conclusion, and uphold the conclusion anyway (“although”, “despite”, “however much”).

EstructuraEjemploNotas
Much as + subject + verbMuch as I admire her courage, I cannot support the decision.“However much…”; with verbs of feeling and judgement.
Verb / adjective / noun + as + subject + may/might/beTry as they might, they couldn't change the system. Strange as it may seem, … Young as she was, …Emphatic fronting; no article (Child though he was).
However + adj / adv; Whatever, Whoever, No matter howHowever hard he works, he never gets ahead.“However + adjective…”; however is attached to its adjective.
Be that as it may; Granted (that); AdmittedlyBe that as it may, we still have to meet the deadline.Global concession that departs from the previous argument.
Albeit + adjective / adverb / phraseThe reform was a success, albeit a limited one.Formal; does not take a subject and a conjugated verb.
Notwithstanding / Despite / In spite of + noun or -ingDespite the criticism, the project went ahead.Despite of does not exist.
Although / Even though / Though + clause; While / Whereas (contrast)Although he was tired, he kept working.Never combined with but in the same sentence.

watch.wrong: Although he was tired, but he continued working.
watch.right: Although he was tired, he continued working.
watch.why: Although and but are not used together; the Spanish “aunque… pero” is acceptable, but not in English.

watch.wrong: Despite of the criticism, the project went ahead.
watch.right: Despite the criticism, the project went ahead.
watch.why: Despite does not take of; In spite of does.

watch.wrong: The reform worked, albeit it was limited.
watch.right: The reform worked, albeit to a limited extent.
watch.why: Albeit is used with an adjective, adverb or phrase, not with a conjugated verb.

watch.wrong: However he tries hard, he never succeeds.
watch.right: However hard he tries, he never succeeds.
watch.why: However + adjective/adverb together at the start.

learn.title: Formulas for summarising, presenting and reflecting
learn.html:
• I'd like to begin by … / I want to start with a question. — opening a presentation.
  • This brings me to … / Let me turn to … — moving on to the next point.
  • What strikes me most is … — introducing a personal observation with a cleft sentence.
  • Looking back, … / In hindsight, … — evaluating the past; they often go with mixed conditionals.
  • It would be a mistake to assume that … — qualifying carefully.
  • Not only … but also … — adding arguments with emphasis.
  • Taking everything into account, … / To sum up, … — closing with a summary.
  • What remains to be seen is whether … — leaving a question open.
  • I'll leave you with one thought: … — cierre memorable.

write.prompt: Write a reflective essay of 300 to 400 words: “What has changed and what has stayed the same in my life as a learner (of English, of a profession or of a city)?” Combine narrative, analysis and a nuanced conclusion. It must include at least: an inversion (Rarely / Not only / Only after…), a cleft sentence, a mixed conditional, a mandative subjunctive and a concessive (Much as / Try as … might / Albeit).
checklist: A correct inversion with a negative adverb or Only/Not until
A cleft sentence (It was… that / What … is)
A mixed or inverted conditional (Had I… / If I had …, I would be …)
A mandative subjunctive or if I were / as if + were
A concessive (Much as… / Try as … might / Albeit…)
At least one proverb or allusion used naturally
Clear introduction, development and conclusion; between 300 and 400 words
write.model:
Rarely do I think about how much has changed since I first opened an English textbook, yet the distance travelled is considerable. Ten years ago I could barely order a coffee in English; today I write essays, argue in meetings and, on good days, even joke. Change, however, is only half the story, because some things have remained stubbornly the same.

What has changed most is my attitude to mistakes. Not only did I once fear them, I also took them as proof of inadequacy. Only after a teacher pointed out that fluency is built on error did I begin to relax. It was that remark, more than any grammar rule, that unlocked my speaking. If I had not met her, I would still be waiting for perfection before I opened my mouth, and my English would be far poorer for it. Much as I would like to claim a steady upward curve, the truth is more uneven: progress came in bursts, followed by long plateaus.

What has stayed the same is the role of curiosity. It is my need to know why a phrase is used, not the quantity of vocabulary I have memorised, that drives my learning. Try as I might to turn study into a routine, I always end up following a question down a rabbit hole. I suspect that if I were more disciplined, I would learn faster; but I doubt I would enjoy it, and enjoyment is what keeps me going.

It is essential that learners be allowed to find their own rhythm. Insisting that everyone follow the same path is, to borrow an old proverb, like trying to make a horse drink: you can lead it to water, but you cannot force it. Albeit slow, my own route has taught me patience.

Looking back, then, the more things change, the more they stay the same: the languages, the tools and the teachers have changed, but the learner behind them has not. And that, I think, is reassuring.

write.prompt: Write the script for a 3-minute oral presentation (300 to 400 words) titled “Change and continuity in my country over the last twenty years”. Use opening, transition and closing formulas; include a cautious prediction and at least one point you concede to the opposing view. Keep a formal but lively register.
targets: vocabulary of social and technological change
checklist: An opening that grabs attention (I'd like to begin by… / a question)
Two transitions (This brings me to… / Let me turn to…)
At least two advanced structures (inversion, cleft sentence, concessive, subjunctive)
Vocabulary of change and technology (tipping point, entrenched, obsolete, digital divide…)
A cautious prediction (might well / is likely to / It would be a mistake to assume…)
A memorable close (I'll leave you with one thought…)
Between 300 and 400 words
write.model:
Good morning, everyone. I'd like to begin with a question: if someone had fallen asleep in Mexico in 2004 and woken up today, what would astonish them most? The answer, I think, is not what we might expect.

Let me start with the obvious. Technology has transformed daily life. Rarely did anyone in 2004 pay a bill from a phone; today it is unremarkable. Mobile banking, delivery apps and video calls have reached places that were once cut off, and the smartphone has become, for many families, the only computer they own. That, however, is where the digital divide becomes visible: it is in rural areas that connections remain slow and costly, and the benefits are unevenly shared.

This brings me to a second change, in how we work. Remote work, once a curiosity, is now entrenched in many sectors, and the traditional office is no longer the default. Much as I welcome this flexibility, I would be the first to admit that it has left some people isolated.

Let me turn now to what has not changed. It is the family that remains the centre of social life. Sunday lunches, endless cousins and the habit of arriving late to everything have survived every wave of innovation. What strikes me is that technology has not replaced these customs; it has simply carried them onto screens, where grandparents now join the family table by video.

Admittedly, not everything has moved in a good direction. Inequality persists, and some industries have become obsolete almost overnight, leaving workers behind. I would not wish to suggest that progress has been painless.

So where might we be in another twenty years? It would be a mistake to assume that the next changes will resemble the last. Artificial intelligence might well reshape work as profoundly as the mobile phone reshaped communication, and we are likely to reach another tipping point sooner than we expect.

I'll leave you with one thought. Countries, like people, change their tools far faster than they change their habits. The challenge for the next generation will be to choose which of the two deserves to be kept. Thank you.

reading.title: The Last Typewriter Repair Shop
reading.intro: Read the feature article and answer. Notice how the author combines anecdote, history and reflection.
paragraphs: On the corner of Calle Allende, between a phone-repair kiosk and a shop that sells nothing but phone cases, there is a narrow door whose sign has faded almost beyond reading. "Typewriters & Calculators: Repairs", it says. Few people go in. Fewer still know that the man behind the counter, Don Ernesto, has fixed machines in this room for fifty-three years, and that he can tell what is wrong with a stuck carriage merely by listening to it.

It would be easy to cast him as a relic, and it is a temptation that journalists have rarely resisted. A television crew visited last spring, filmed the dust and the brass levers, and left with a charming little report about "vanishing trades". What the report failed to mention is that the shop has not been losing money. Not only has business held steady; it has, in the last three years, quietly grown. Few of his new customers are nostalgic pensioners. Most are students, novelists and a surprising number of office workers who say, in one form or another, that they simply cannot think on a screen.

Ernesto himself is sceptical of the romance. "People say the typewriter is back," he told me, wiping his hands on a cloth, "but it never really left. What has happened is that the world got louder, and some people went looking for quiet." He was not always so calm about it. When the first personal computers arrived in the early nineties, he assumed that his trade would be dead within a decade. Had he followed his own prediction, he would have closed the shop and retrained as an electrician, as his brother urged him to. Much as he regrets the years of worry, he concedes that the scare taught him to diversify: he now repairs sewing machines, mechanical clocks and, to his own amusement, the occasional vinyl turntable.

The pattern he describes is familiar to historians of technology, who have long observed that old tools seldom disappear outright. Rather, they are displaced from the centre of life to its edges, where they survive for those who value what they do differently. Radio did not kill the newspaper, nor did television kill radio, though each, in turn, was confidently expected to. Were every prophecy of extinction borne out, we would by now be living in a world with no books, no cinemas and no letters. Technologies do not so much replace one another as rearrange themselves, and the rearrangement is rarely complete.

None of this means that nothing changes. Ernesto's apprentice, a twenty-three-year-old named Luz, learned the trade from videos before she ever touched a machine, and she posts her repairs online, where they are watched by thousands of strangers in countries Ernesto could not find on a map. It was her idea, not his, to start selling restored typewriters over the internet. "At first I objected," he admits. "I said it was a betrayal. Then the first crate went to Oslo, and I understood that the thing I was defending was not the shop. It was the work."

Perhaps that is the lesson hidden in this corner of the city. Change is rarely the clean break that headlines promise; it is a negotiation between what a society is ready to abandon and what it cannot bear to lose. The more things change, the old French proverb has it, the more they stay the same, though it would be more accurate to say that they stay the same only because someone, somewhere, is patient enough to keep them going. Were it not for people like Ernesto and Luz, continuity would be little more than a word. As the afternoon light falls across the workbench, he lifts a typewriter's carriage, listens, and smiles. Old habits, he says, die hard; and so, it seems, do the things worth keeping.

listening.title: Open Question: does technology change us?
listening.intro: Listen to the radio debate between a presenter, a sociologist and an engineer. You can replay it.

lines.text: Welcome back to Open Question. Tonight's topic: does new technology change society, or does society simply bend technology to its own habits? With me are sociologist Dr Rahman and software engineer Tom Whitfield. Dr Rahman, you first.

Thank you. I'd say the answer is both, but the second half is usually forgotten. Rarely does a technology arrive and impose a single outcome. What happens is that people adapt it in ways its inventors never imagined.
I'd agree, up to a point. Take text messaging. Little did the engineers know that it would become the main way teenagers talked. It was a feature meant for network technicians.
So what you're saying is that users, not designers, write the real manual?
Precisely. Though, much as I admire the ingenuity of users, I don't want to romanticise it. Not only can technology amplify our best habits, it can entrench our worst ones.
Granted. Recommendation algorithms are a case in point. Had we foreseen how they'd shape what people read, we would have built them differently. But hindsight is easy.
Tom, is it fair to say the industry was careless?
Careless, perhaps; malicious, no. Be that as it may, the effects are real, and it is vital that engineers be held accountable for them.
I'd go further. It's essential that these systems be audited by people with no financial stake in them. Under no circumstances should a company mark its own homework.
Is there a risk, though, that we regulate too early and strangle innovation?

There's always that risk. But the reason why regulation tends to arrive late is that nobody wants to be first. If we'd acted when the warning signs first appeared, we'd be having a very different conversation today.
I'd rather we proceeded with caution than waited for a disaster. Don't throw the baby out with the bathwater, though. Some of this technology has genuinely saved lives.
A fair note to end on. Old habits die hard, but perhaps new ones can form. Dr Rahman, Tom, thank you both.
Thank you. It's been a pleasure.
